results.title: What Is Endogeneity? What Is An Exogenous Variable? - Science ABC
results.content: What Is An Exogenous Variable? * What Is An Exogenous Variable? > Endogeneity is a variable or change that arises internally from a model or system. An exogenous variable is a variable that is not affected by other variables, but will affect other variables of the system. Endogeneity is a variable or change that arises internally from a model or system. The amount of product (cotton thread) is the endogenous variable and is dependent on a number of other variables, which include weather around the cotton fields, price of fuel and other transportation costs of the process, pests and pesticides used to counter them and their cost, etc. This dependence makes it an endogenous variable. Do Purely Endogenous Variables Even Exist? It’s more likely that endogenous variables are only partially endogenous and simultaneously determined by exogenous factors. For example, cotton production is affected by pests, and pests are affected by changes in weather. Therefore, pests in this system are partially endogenous and partially exogenous, making cotton production a partially exogenous and endogenous variable at the same time. What Is An Exogenous Variable? An exogenous variable is a variable that is not affected by other variables, but will affect other variables of the system. Factors like farmer skill, weather, and the availability of seed are all exogenous to crop production. Therefore, to see a perfectly endogenous or exogenous variable is a rarity. Unlike independent variables and dependent variables in an experiment, identifying which variables are exogenous, and which are endogenous, can pose a challenge due to their confusing relations with other variables in the system. In order to decide if this new variable is exogenous, you would have to decide if the increase in output would cause the new variables to change. A variable like “weather” is definitely exogenous, as a rise in output would have no effect on the weather. The price of the threads produced isn’t affected by one small manufacturing plant’s output, but what if this was the biggest manufacturing plant in the world that suddenly increased its production, resulting in a saturated market? In this case, price would be partially an endogenous variable and partially an exogenous one.
